It provides an in-depth analysis of these models' behavior as both the interaction range and a parameter t approach zero, highlighting how these limits can be significant for nonlocal-to-local model transitions in applications. Most of the integral models relate to their corresponding local PDE counterparts, and this article explores which properties are preserved during this transition. It also discusses the conditions under which the interaction density converges to either fractional or classical diffusion equations. Notably, it shows how certain model features, such as nonmonotone solutions, are inherited from their local counterparts and how some models can lead to unrealistic predictions due to unphysical long-tail asymptotic behavior.

When multiple videos are recorded on different surfaces but relate to the same scene from different viewpoints, creating a single comprehensive panoramic image is challenging due to the lack of a common reference point and varying gravity orientations in each video. To overcome this, we propose a technique to automatically align the videos by determining their respective viewing angles and combining them into a single coherent image. A key innovation in our approach is the incorporation of gravity information to constrain the possible solutions and improve efficiency. By solving a system of equations given priority to gravity data, we can determine the minimal solutions that satisfy the requirements given the available information. Ultimately, our approach enables us to capture a single comprehensive panoramic image from multi-planar videos given the available videos and their respective gravity information.

This study establishes essential groundwork for combining Bessel functions across an entire family of Eisenstein series for a general group $GL(n,\mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q})$. Specifically, we examine the behavior near a cutoff sphere in the group's domain of definition for a particular type of Eisenstein series constructed from a parabolic subgroup, defined by a block matrix, and based on an automorphic form for a general linear group. The analysis contributes to Bessel function decomposition efforts as described in the accompanying text for $GL(n,\mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q})$.

This study develops a novel biophysical brain model for Parkinson's disease, utilizing an existing primate brain atlas and incorporating data from marmoset monkeys.  A key feature of this model is its ability to incorporate the effects of deep brain stimulation, making it highly adaptable to research and development purposes. To streamline the creation of such models, a new open-source Python framework called CaSkEr has been designed, utilizing the open-source software Chainmail. This approach does not depend on proprietary formats, and as a result, enables the integration of primate brain data from multiple sources. As demonstrated in this study, computational models of biological systems benefit greatly from open-source tools, and from releasing the model data and code publicly, and it would be in our interest to promote collaboration within the scientific community. Finally, this model and associated code is available for download from the online repository at https://github.com/AnilSharma17/casker-pd-fb-ma.

This research proposes a novel, efficient method for rendering line joins on vector graphics, utilizing simple pixel operations to achieve high performance on mobile devices. The technique balances rendering speed and visual accuracy, making it versatile for various purposes. As a result, the method has been successfully applied in multiple map applications, including OneMap, SeaMap, and WebMap, on mobile platforms.

We have completed a preliminary study of nine gas kinematics at sub-second arcsecond resolution using the KOOLS-IFU on Seimei Telescope, which we used to observe nine gas giant galaxies at distances less than 0.04 astronomical units. These galaxies are going through a major star formation process, which is fueled by a merging process, and we found that their gas velocities are heavily influenced by outflows from supernovae. This study represents an initial exploration of the impact of star formation processes on gas kinematics, and it will be expanded in the future to gain more comprehensive insights into the gas kinematics of these galaxies.

The multivariate interpolation operator is traditionally constructed using piecewise linear functions to approximate absolute differences between values. In this study, we develop a novel, transcendental interpolation function based on the Cauchy exponential function, which establishes a precise connection between linear interpolation and scalar interpolation. Subsequently, we integrate this function into a set of multivariate interpolation operators utilizing the Cauchy exponential function and a positive definite radial basis function, thereby establishing the relationship between linear interpolation and scalar interpolation in multiple dimensions. Furthermore, we establish convergence criteria for our scheme and demonstrate its ability to preserve the original function's characteristics.

Advances in deep learning and computer vision have driven the development of intelligent systems capable of analyzing and interpreting visual data, in particular, weather recognition from images is an essential step towards autonomous vehicles safely navigating through various weather conditions.  This project aims to create a robust system weather classifier that can assess the external environment and predict the weather, specifically sun, overcast, rain, and snow weather from images.  A novel dataset containing 12000 images was created and released containing all four weather conditions and evaluated multiple state-of-the-art classifiers, in addition to developing a suitable data augmentation technique to tackle the dataset's class imbalance problem.  Experimental results demonstrated that the proposed system outperformed competing approaches and successfully handled diverse scenarios, in particular providing accurate weather predictions, outperforming the industry standard algorithm by 7% improvement rate.  Our system provides a highly efficient and reliable weather classification system and can serve as an excellent benchmark for future research in this domain.

Multi-channel audio separation models are generally superior to single-channel models and are widely accepted, nevertheless, they demand additional hardware to capture mixed sources and fail to address scenarios where only a single mixed audio input is available. To overcome this limitation, we propose a novel single-channel audio separation model called DPCRN, which is an innovative architecture that combines dual paths of convolution recurrent networks. This model is capable of producing satisfactory results without the need for phase loss compensation, and is built upon a single mixed audio input, which is sequence-dependent and single channel audio. DPCRN is trained to output the missing spectral components of the target source and has been tested on the Microsoft Dataset 32c, demonstrating state-of-the-art performance in difficult conditions without the use of phase loss compensation.

Our computational model integrates non-relativistic $f(R)$ gravity with massive neutrinos to explore their combined impacts on the turn-around radii of dark matter halos. Using a linear perturbation theory to examine how structure forms in an $f(R)$ gravity context, we discovered that modified gravity increases structure formation, while neutrinos with their large wavelengths suppress it due to their inability to clump together. By adjusting model parameters and applying the Halo Finder technique to identify the boundary where the expansion of space overcomes gravitational attraction, we determined our model's capacity to accurately predict turn-around radii. Notably, to counter the clumping effects of 10 keV neutrinos at a specific $f_R$ value, a $10^{12} M_\odot$ halo, we found necessary adjustments in the $f_R$ parameter could achieve this balance.

This research is a first in single-column modeling using a two-fluid approach, as a two-fluid framework single-column model is thoroughly analyzed to establish a foundation for developing two-fluid three-dimensional models of atmospheric convection. A two-fluid framework consists of two overlapping air masses under the influence of gravity that generate convection currents, radiate, and are subject to temperature and friction-induced wall effects. Key features of atmospheric convection, including the development of boundary layers, internal layer mixtures, and multi-periodic pulsations are simulated and compared to established theoretical models and observations. The model successfully simulates the characteristics of air flows in both the viscous and thermal boundary layers and internal layers. The success of this single-column model paves the way for a two-fluid three-dimensional model of atmospheric convection.

We analyze a system of two separately correlated atoms, each interacting with different modes that are initially unrelated. Under specific circumstances, we discover that the atoms become genuinely entangled without any need for post-selection. Notably, the intensity of this entanglement increases as the uncertainty in one of the modes rises. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this approach achieves maximum accuracy in estimating one of the quantum parameters when entanglement reaches its peak. Interestingly, our analysis also reveals that using uncorrelated resources can yield the same entropy as would have been attained with correlated (displaced) modes, resulting in more efficient use of quantum resources.

The CMS experiment's interactive database system relies heavily on identifying and tracking particles, with an emphasis on finding muon endpoints and jet trajectories. Approximately 90% of trajectory data comes from tracks reconstructed in the pixel detector. However, in 2022, the LHC will undergo a high luminosity upgrade, necessitating an examination of trajectory reconstruction methods. To prepare for this upgrade, researchers are utilizing the phase-1 pixel detector system, which operates under different detection conditions and data processing speeds. A critical component of this system is the identification of track trajectories, particularly at certain strategic locations known as pilot blades. This study investigates the reconstruction of these pilot tracks by comparing them to full tracks and determining any biases in track parameter measurements, with a focus on navigating complex particle interactions and forward jets. The results of this examination are presented in this paper.

We present a method for creating a Kall\'en-Lehmann spectral representation of the SU(2) gluonium spectrum in scalar channels, without requiring a gauge-fixing procedure. This approach is based on the correlation of two non-local gauge-invariant operators and we provide an algorithm to calculate the spectral function from lattice QCD data, which we employ to estimate the gluonium spectrum using simulated data from an effective theory, as well as direct lattice calculations of the spectrum. These calculations yield estimates for the two-particle threshold at $6.04(9)(6)$ GeV and a spectrum of $6.04(9)(6)$ GeV, $6.77(18)(10)$ GeV, and $7.13(20)(12)$ GeV. The reliability of our method is verified by successfully predicting the quarkonium spectrum from nucleon data, and the results for the gluonium are presented for states $gg$, $s\bar{c}$ and $cc$, which include the charmonium and bottomonium spectra. The lattice determination of the spectrum is illustrated for $gg$, $s\bar{c}$ and $cc$, and the results for the gluonium are given as $6.04(9)(6)$ GeV, $6.77(18)(10)$ GeV, and $7.13(20)(12)$ GeV.

Social media monitoring through sentiment analysis on platforms like Twitter enables a monitoring account to determine the general emotions of its followers. To accomplish this, we need to determine the emotional reactions of users in their posts on Twitter. We are able to determine the general emotions of users by combining the individual emotions expressed in their posts. On Twitter, expressing a liking, loving, or disapproving of a post can significantly influence the expression of sentiment. Additionally, we need to differentiate between different uses of words to accurately express sentiment. For example, "great" can be used to express a positive sentiment, but it can also be used to express a negative sentiment, as in "I hate this great post". We present a method for analyzing the sentiment of a tweet using a combination of features, which feeds into an LSTM network that is trained to output the emotional reaction of a user. We are able to convert a tweet to a sequence of words using Natural Language Tools, and then we process this sequence to extract contextual features from each word using BERT. We also use a Twitter analyzer to retrieve entities, hashtags, and punctuation, and we convert these entities to emotional reactions. These numerical features are combined and used to create the input for our LSTM network. Through the use of this method, we are able to accurately classify the emotional reaction of a user in their post.

A nonlinear, charge-based scalar field is employed to describe a charged black hole in four-dimensional Anti-de Sitter space. A line of shade spheres surrounding the event horizon creates a boundary between the black hole and an outer region, creating a shaded region. A line of probe particles at the base of the shade produces a lever arm length. Using a 3D integral over the shade, the thermodynamic volume is calculated and verified through analytical and numerical methods for various nonlinear parameters. The relationship between the thermodynamic volume, mass, and charge of the black hole in an unsaturated state is explored through charts and reveals a non-monotonic behavior.

Quantum operations can lead to the growth of entanglement between previously uncorrelated subsystems, ultimately facilitating a transition to a synchronized state. To numerically evaluate these phenomena using uncorrelated qubits and a two-qubit Heisenberg chain, we proposed a novel approach that leverages both traditional and innovative tomograms, incorporating a success function akin to a fidelity measure. Our approach yielded accurate results for Heisenberg entanglement and onset, even when only one qubit became entangled. Furthermore, we demonstrated that tomograms for the Grover algorithm reveal a clear entonic profile.

Building a chatbot that adheres to a particular role while having the flexibility to discuss any topic is both challenging and vital for a language model to master. This study aims to explore a model that is constrained by a specific role specification, yet capable of covering any subject matter. It seeks to answer two key questions: (1) the effectiveness of leveraging a large-scale language model to create a role-constrained specification system, and (1) the methods to guide the model to stay within the designated role through a specific construction approach.

Agricultural production, significantly influenced by pests, poses a critical threat to food output, necessitating a balanced approach to disease management that considers both yield and environmental sustainability. Agricultural decisions, inherently uncertain due to varying weather conditions, pest behavior, and product prices, require a meticulous evaluation process. This process involves comparing the risk of different management options through a method that accounts for best and worst-case scenarios, weighted by probability, to guide more informed and stable choices. We introduce a rigorous assessment framework for pest management, test its efficacy with strawberry disease management, and yield insights suggesting that investing in integrated pest management, despite its initial cost, results in a more stable return, demonstrating the value of this approach for achieving sustainable agricultural outcomes.

In the creation of 360-degree virtual tours, aligning adjacent panoramic images to reconstruct a three-dimensional scene from a video requires accurate perspective prediction. This task is particularly challenging when dealing with video underwater footage due to the varying lighting and water currents that affect underwater photography. We have developed a novel approach that utilizes subtitles as unique, human-annotated reference points to guide perspective prediction. By combining a subtitle-aware hierarchical transformer with a hierarchical cosine predictor, our SubAria model leverages both subtitle information and image content for more accurate perspective prediction. Our SubAria model has been shown to significantly improve virtual tourism video quality, and we make it available along with evaluation metrics on newly released underwater datasets IP-Underwater and UnderwaterTour.

We enhance the TEDOS and PEPS representations of time evolution and thermal states in systems with open boundaries through localized deformations, yielding more accurate results for observable calculations. These improvements significantly lower the scaling of errors with bond dimension, particularly when simulating systems in the diffusive regime. Notably, thermal states are captured most effectively away from system edges. Additionally, our method integrates seamlessly with the TEDOS algorithm to thermalize initial states via repeated applications, achieving substantial reductions in time-observable error. Our findings provide valuable insights into the varied reliance of time- and thermal-procedures on boundary conditions based on their underlying physics.

We develop a decoupling approach to address situations where an agent's influence on a target is both limited and varying in intensity in relation to a target. This proposed framework is applicable to problems of classification, regulation, and prediction. We achieve this by creating both accurate and biased approximations of a restriction, and through experimentation, it demonstrates improved performance over existing methods.

We investigate anisotropic p-capacitance related to norms in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$, deriving a deep connection with anisotropic mean curvature through capacitance variation. This relationship enables us to prove the anisotropic Minkowski inequality for convex bodies in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The Microscope space test for the weak equivalence principle relies on precise measurements of two test masses in a microgravity environment. Understanding and minimizing instrumental noise is crucial, especially sudden shifts in signal known as glitches. These can have an unexpected impact on the experimental outcome and should be carefully managed, particularly given the extended 14-day measurement period. We examine the distribution of glitch sizes and their frequency, as well as their influence on the result and potential improvements. Different strategies for handling glitches are evaluated through simulation and actual data analysis. We also investigate the relationship between glitch characteristics and frequency, and their potential cause may be traced to temperature changes. This understanding can help design better instrumentation for future tests.

We examine a pair of spherical particles whose interaction with one another fluctuates randomly, subject to an activity gradient that affects them. This study reveals how varying levels of external drive influence the pair's behavior, including its ability to move through spaces and collect information, and explores the connection between activity levels and different conformational states. Our findings demonstrate that greater levels of external stimulation can result in a more compact form and altered network collection patterns. To better understand these phenomena, we developed simple models that account for changes in motion, volume accessibility, and the ability to collect objects based on applicable geometry. Furthermore, our simulations and theoretical analysis provide insights into the electronic density of states and the impact of activity levels on the pair's morphological structure.

This paper defines a new concept, the strong shortest path collection, for graphs and determines some graphs that have this property, including K4,3 and K3,3,3. It also explores cacti and certain triod graphs to calculate their strong shortest path collections. Additionally, the paper introduces a related concept, the k-strong shortest path collection, and provides a definition for infinite graphs. A specific criterion for infinite graphs to meet this new criterion is also established.

A nonperturbative renormalon has been identified in the series of perturbative corrections within the color dipole gluon TMD PDF framework at small-$x$, and it is located approximately 2$\Lambda_{\rm QCD}^2$ in the BML variable space. This finding suggests a possible connection between the renormalon in the perturbative impact parameter expansion and the perturbative DGLAP asymptotic behavior. Moreover, considering the distinct spacely scales associated with both regimes, the equality of these spacely scales may account for the complex, non-interchangeable relationship observed between perturbative DGLAP and BML evolutions in practical applications.
As anticipated by the recent findings of Tóth and Westwater, the speed at which the frog model behaves supercritically on a tree is directly proportional to the tree's height.

Researchers are focusing on nonreciprocal light control through the use of magnetophotonic structures, but designing these structures to modify light in desired directions while minimizing sensitivity to its initial orientation is challenging. In this study, we engineered a novel type of structure consisting of two layers of coupled surfaces with multiple magnetic inclusions that can modify group and phase velocities of light traveling in different directions separately. By adjusting the proportion of surfaces receiving magnetic influence, we are able to achieve significant velocity differences for light moving in opposite directions. Notably, a specific configuration grants complete transmission only to light moving a particular direction and blocks transmission of light moving the contrary direction. This discovery paves the way for highly compact nonreciprocal devices with miniscule loss.

A pioneering approach was introduced for using a pre-trained artificial neural network (ANN) that has been trained on a decision-making model known as a black-box. This innovative approach allows for a form of decision-making analysis to be performed without the need for extensive data collection. When applied to a decision-making model (DMM) whose internal workings are not fully understood, this approach enables a pre-trained ANN to accurately replicate the performance of the decision-making model and, in some cases, provide a more efficient version. Notably, this decision-transfer technique requires only a limited amount of input, no access to the actual black-box model, and, when it comes to decision transfer, also needs very few targeted evaluations. When applied to a decision-making model (DMM) based on a neural network, this approach results in a significant reduction in size of the pre-trained ANN. When applied to a decision-making model (DMM) based on a decision tree, it offers a more effective version with a substantial decrease in performance loss. When applied to a decision-making model (DMM) based on a support vector machine, it creates a more effective version with a significant reduction in training time. This approach was demonstrated with a variety of decision-making models (DMMs) and a collection of benchmark datasets.

Researchers have studied the decay of $B^0_s$ particles into $\bar{D}^{*0,0}$ particles and $K^0_S$ particles, obtaining measurements of the decay probability which are $4.98 \pm 0.48 \times 10^{-4}$ and $2.49 \pm 0.28 \pm 0.11 \times 10^{-4}$ respectively, based on a large dataset collected by the LHCb experiment. Additionally, they have also presented initial evidence for the latter decay mode.

We present a novel algorithm for constructing the lattice of submodules within any multiplicity-free module over a distributive lattice. This construction method bypasses the need for computing all intermediate submodules. Our algorithm builds the lattice of submodules from a given set of submodules, applying Rees' theorem to establish an isomorphism between the lattice of submodules and a lattice of congruences of the given set of submodules. We outline the details of this construction in ReesLattice which can be found at https://github.com/dmitry-ivanchenko/ReesLattice.

A graph is considered geodetic if there's only one shortest path between any two of its vertices. This paper introduces a search-based method to determine if a given graph is geodetic. Our method builds on a recently proposed concept called the Robust Geodetic Characterization (RGC) of a graph. Specifically, it proposes an algorithm to identify whether a graph is geodetic based on its RGC, or concludes that such an RGC does not exist. Notably, finding an n-vertex graph's RGC may result in an graph with a significantly larger number of vertices. As a consequence, determining if a given graph possesses an RGC is not limited to small graphs. It's also worth mentioning that certain classes of geodetic graphs can be characterized by a single vertex addition or a specific graph property called a geodetic set. However, research has revealed that determining if a general graph contains a geodetic set of a particular size or with a specific number of edges cannot be efficiently solved. Based on these solutions and limitations, we provide insights into computing a given graph's geodetic number or determining if it contains a geodetic set of a particular size or edge count. This work paves the way for significant advancements in solving these problems for a wide range of practical graphs.

In imitation learning, a robot aims to master a task by observing a teacher's actions. However, when the provided demonstrations are scarce, generalization becomes a major hurdle. To tackle this issue, researchers have devised various inference methods capable of utilizing suboptimal and sparse demonstration data. Despite these advancements, tries to generalize beyond the demonstration range remain largely unsuccessful using typical reward-based approaches. This paper proposes a novel algorithm that achieves generalization beyond the demonstration range. It achieves this by learning a concise policy from the demonstrations and transferring it to the target environment. Our method presents theoretical advantages over current state-of-the-art techniques and is supported by experimental evidence showing its superiority in efficient sample usage.

Multi-teacher learning is an effective strategy for generating high-quality data and teaching multiple instructors to teach students. To train a single student, it's common to let them observe multiple instructors demonstrating how to complete a task, and select the best one. In contrast, there's no standard method to use a single student to learn from multiple teachers simultaneously. In this work, we develop a novel framework to utilize the potential of student data by enabling it to learn co-imitation from observations of two agents performing the same task. By introducing an innovative loss function, our framework allows agents to learn characteristics from data that represent typical movements, boundary cases, and underlying task semantics. As a result, it produces robust and consistent data and performance. To validate this, we conducted experiments on a table pushing task and found that our method outperformed existing single and dual teacher training methods when only boundary data was used.

This research addresses the calculation of the metric for peaceful coding codes, utilizing a specific coding scheme for compact digital-analog-digital (CAD) converters that can be easily understood. The proposed method involves a simplified analysis of code distance, utilizing an adjusted linear metric that accounts for the impact of analog errors, considering the effect of the final stage's rounding. The method is specifically applied to determine the distortion and resolution of intermediate-fixed point (IFP) converters. The results show that the calculation of the metric and peaceful coding codes can be efficiently achieved. The proposed method is then demonstrated through reference to a research study on the performance of a two-stage IFP converter.

Previous studies have combined translation selection selection (TSS) and reinforcement learning (RFT) to improve evaluation metrics beyond likelihood. However, their application to languages with large vocabularies remains limited. We utilized a sequential reinforcement learning approach to train a neural machine translation model that is ordered. We designed a new framework called SARL-NS to allow for a vast action space by employing a discrete vocabulary for target languages. The framework leverages a action-space reduction technique to streamline the translation process. We tested our framework on English to Japanese and English to German. Experimental results show that our method successfully produces high-quality translations, outperforming previous RL-based methods on languages with large vocabularies.

A popular and versatile robot setup involves a depth camera mounted on a robotic arm. This camera is responsible for identifying objects in the environment and on nearby surfaces. For it to function properly, the relationship between the robot's base and the camera needs to be determined, as well as the pose of the arm's end-effector. A human can provide this information using special markers and symbols. However, using markers increases the cost and makes it harder to attach and remove the camera. A method is required to learn this relationship automatically without using special markers. A method is also required to estimate the pose of the end-effector based on a regular image, rather than relying on special symbols. This paper presents a method to extract the camera parameters from an image, and requires only a few special symbols to provide initial data. This paper also explores the possibility of improving end-effector pose estimation using a special technique called a pose classifier. A method is proposed to train this classifier with a limited amount of special symbols. However, attaching and detaching the camera to different parts of the arm is quite difficult. Therefore, a method to estimate the pose of the end-effector based on a regular image is proposed instead. This paper evaluates this method on a real arm and finds it to be more accurate than other methods. A method is proposed to refine this approach and obtain highly accurate results on a real arm.

We introduce a new concept called the QFS-region (quasiperiodic steady state region) for high-dimensional time series, which is a method for identifying the dimension of the system's state space. We provide an explanation of QFS-region, along with a relevant theory and a method to estimate the system's intrinsic dimension. A numerical experiment demonstrates the effectiveness of this approach. Building on this, we introduce two novel concepts, the causal QFS-region and the total QFS-region, and explore their relationships with the QFS-region. These ideas are then applied to analyze complex systems, such as the quiescent/funicular state of a bridge and a time-series dataset.

The analysis of online news consumption data from the Google News service,
obtained between 2010 and 2018, employed UMAP for visualisation and community
detection through the Louvain algorithm to map reader preferences and explore
their changes over time. Initially, viewerers were segmented into four primary
groups based on device usage - mobile, desktop, or both, or neither - with
mobile users displaying distinct political consumption patterns compared to
desktop users. On average, viewerers were divided into approximately
hundred community clusters with varying sizes, predominantly composed of
smaller communities, while approximately thirty large communities reflected
broadly popular topics such as major sports events, popular television shows,
and coronavirus-related information. With mobile news consumption patterns
being more diverse than those of desktop users, desktop users exhibited more
significant changes over time with the emergence of numerous new, small
communities. Notably, we observed an increase in political division among
online news readers, with mobile users experiencing this trend in about thirty
large communities and desktop users in roughly fifty.

We make significant progress on classifying the language complexity of subgroups within the Thompson group V, specifically for groups formed by finite index subgroupst. Our findings indicate that these subgroups can have a wide range of sentence complexity types, including those unsolvable, and we provide an intermediate category. Additionally, for this particular intermediate category, we establish a distinct thermal-like pattern.

We examined a driven two-level system and found that, under certain non-equilibrium conditions created by periodic microwave signals and thermalized by phonons, it reaches a steady state independent of time. This non-equilibrium thermal steady state can be thought of as two separate thermalizations occurring at different scales. Key features of this condition were experimentally identified through a real qubit experiment, and and a theoretical model developed. This model predicts that, at a specific driving frequency, the non-equilibrium thermal steady state condition emerges. It also allows estimation of the thermal phonon bath temperature and Rabi rotation angle from measurable factors.

This research explores several advanced submanifold structures in Euclidean space, including those with varying curvature properties and geometric relationships. Specifically, it focuses on biharmonic hypersurfaces and implements several recurrent mechanisms, such as conformal, cosymplectic, and semi-Riemannian structures. By applying these mechanisms, it demonstrates that certain configurations lead to minimal hypersurfaces, while others result in contradictory outcomes. Furthermore, it investigates hypersurfaces defined by n-parallism and pseudo-n-parallism, showing that any such biharmonic hypersurface is actually a minimal one. Finally, it establishes that a specific type of hypersurface, known as a pseudo-柏格流形, cannot contain biharmonic elements.

Let idlp(p,q) denote the smallest number of queries (with responses being positive integers) that make a pair of distinct fractions p/l and q/l (where q > p > 0 and l is a positive integer) stand out from any other fraction p'/l'. This concept was first explored by Dr. G. K. S. (1967) when he examined the properties of these numbers (or infinity) for specific values of p, q, and their relationship to the multiplicative order of (p/q) (p/q being a reduced fraction and (p/q)|p-q being the multiplicative order of (p/q) (p/q being a reduced fraction and (p/q)|p-q denotes the smallest positive integer such that (p/q)^((p/q)|p-q) = 1 (mod p-q))). In this study, we introduce the ideas of reduced, coprime, and distinct identifiable sets of the form {p/l, q/l, r/l, ...} and define the smallest number of queries needed to distinguish any such set from any other as lp(p1/p2, p3, p4, ...). Furthermore, we establish relationships between lp(p1/p2, p3, p4, ...) and (p1/p2)|p1-p2, provide examples of cases where lp(p1/p2, p3) does not equal (p1/p2)|p1-p2, and introduce binary expansion

Our study explores a theoretical framework that combines axions with sterile neutrinos to form a type of matter called 'shadow dark matter.' In this model, axions decay into pairs of sterile neutrinos via an extended version of the See-Saw type I mechanism. These neutrinos, having masses in an eV range, gradually accumulate in the universe's center as they are gravitationally trapped, gradually building up dark matter halos around galaxies. We analyze whether this model can explain observed phenomena such as the axion decay constant, galaxy rotation curves, and gravitational lensing in a universe that contains 'shadow dark matter.' By estimating the minimum and maximum ranges for the required parameters of the model through these observational constraints, we aim to identify intersections where 'shadow dark matter' could constitute a significant portion (20-40%) of the total dark matter population.

Between October 2020 and April 2021, the LAMOST performed a unique observational study using four K2 plates, which included nearly 3.3 million stars of 20 different functional categories. The LAMOST recorded variations in cross-correlation functions for each star, effectively creating a simplified spectrum. The results showed that the simplified spectrum could identify the properties of the stars, such as their temperature, radius, and maximum oscillation frequency. The calculated errors were under 0.02 for most measurements. The study also revealed that the simplified spectrum could detect changes in radial distances of up to 0.004, which led to the discovery of evolutionary migrations and a water-rich planet with an unusual rotation pattern. The findings were so successful that the simplified spectrum was used to discover a water-world, and it was ranked among the top 5 most significant results in time-domain astronomy globally in 2021. The LAMOST's comprehensive data from this study were made publicly available in 2022.

In image recognition, particularly with two-dimensional images, leveraging prior knowledge about the image analysis technique is commonly practiced. Investigating neighboring pixels along the image boundaries is generally considered less important than in the image's interior. This general principle holds true for three-dimensional images as well. We propose a method to increase model efficiency by employing an odd kernel size near boundaries and either ignoring or decreasing outer layers near images' outer boundaries. This technique, which we call "edge gating," can be integrated into various convolutional neural network architectures. Our experiments on three challenging medical image datasets demonstrate the benefits of edge gating, resulting in improved semantic segmentation results with comparable accuracy to state-of-the-art models but with fewer parameters and reduced computational efficiency.

We utilize a temporal property to assess the correctness of transactional protocols in relation to coherent memory systems. As an example, we examine the transactions protocol of a popular document database, MongoDB, to demonstrate the importance of coherence. Our analysis reveals that MongoDB's protocol fails to guarantee transactional coherence and leads to inconsistent data. We then modify the protocol to rectify these issues and show that our correction achieves optimal performance with minimal additional cost over sequential transaction execution.

Using the elementary symmetric function basis, we re-express the chromatic symmetric functions of Dyck paths with $n-1$ dams for $n \le 9$, and identify an pattern for rewriting any such function. We define a new combinatorial sequence, called inverse Kostka numbers of size $n$, and demonstrate that the coefficients of any Dyck path's chromatic symmetric function, when expressed with $t = 1$, average to the corresponding inverse Kostka numbers for any given size $n$. Additionally, we establish a connection between Inverse Kostka Numbers and the chromatic polynomial.

We explore the concept of function spaces in reinforcement learning, drawing a parallel to cognitive science. Our analysis of function spaces leads us to examine working memory and executive function in the context of reinforcement learning. To model these human capabilities, we develop a multi-task agent that learns through hindsight summarization. This agent uses reinforcement learning to create a decision-making process that maximizes value function efficiency. Specifically, the agent optimizes a policy that minimizes the distance between a source and a target state in a generative Markov decision process. By leveraging reinforcement learning, we hope to shed light on the complex interplay between memory and cognition, or more broadly, executive function. Our experimental results provide empirical evidence that this approach effectively captures key aspects of human working memory and executive function.

The success of deep learning models for medical imaging depends on eliminating inherent biases present in data sets, as these inherent biases can manifest as correlations between certain features and target categories. While researchers have extensively studied gender and racial biases in general medical image data, there is a lack of work on identifying inherent biases in medical core data sets. In this study, we introduce a framework to detect inherent biases and apply it to three widely-used medical core data sets, thereby revealing latent biases present in these data sets.

A well-established theory underpins the study of magnetic materials' complex behaviour, although certain aspects remain unexplained and controversial. Notably, triangular interactions between spins can lead to concealed order when connected in triangles. In this work, a large-scale triangular interaction network was constructed using modular methodology, revealing concealed long-range order and a significant energy barrier that hinders magnetic fluctuations. This concealed dynamics can be manipulated by altering the base triangular interaction's orientation, ultimately enabling a comprehensive understanding of magnetic materials' enigmatic behaviour through the application of abstract algebra.

The innermost region of the solar system has been explored by the Parker Solar Probe since 2018, and as it gradually approaches the Sun, there is an expectation of direct observations of solar breeze, a fluid flowing from the Sun. As this flow moves through solar space, acceleration mechanisms at work can alter the solar breeze speed, flow, and the magnetic field, and these effects must be accounted for in order to understand the solar system. The Parker Solar Probe is uniquely positioned to bypass the narrow shadow region created by the Sun's gravity and measure the solar breeze at various distances from the Sun. As a result, it will provide the most precise measurements of the solar breeze during its 7 close approaches, and these data are expected to reveal fundamental properties of how the solar system functions. In this paper, we present theoretical estimates of the solar breeze and compare them to limited empirical models and early PSP observations. As a result, we find that a key feature of the solar breeze is the presence of the Sonine surface where the solar breeze starts to feel the Sun's pull and may indicate the location of the heliosphere's shock wave. As the PSP closes in on the Sun, we predict that it will observe the point at which the solar breeze is significantly affected and may record signs of this feature. Based on observations made during the first three PSP encounters, we also estimate the magnetic field at 18-49 times stronger than what is normally found at 1 astronomical unit,

Speech emotion recognition is an important application in speech processing and is crucial for intelligent systems to interact effectively with people. A significant challenge in this area is the discrepancy between data collected in controlled environments and interactions with real people. To address this, our research focuses on adapting reinforcement learning models to handle cross-domain speech emotion recognition. By treating this problem as a multi-task learning scenario, we employ a Domain-Adaptive Network to recognize emotions and transfer knowledge between source and target domains. We enhance this approach by using a Domain-Adaptive Module that adapts the learned representations to match the target distribution. Our experiments demonstrate that this proposed method surpasses current state-of-the-art techniques.

We present an investigation of four-layer Aurivillius Bi5FeTi3O15 under high hydrostatic pressure, utilizing X-ray and nuclear forward scattering techniques. At ambient conditions, Bi5FeTi3O15 exhibits simultaneous antiferromagnetic and weak ferromagnetic order, with additional spin canting. Approximately 2 GPa, it transitions to another magnetic phase characterized by altered canting angles and a shift in Bi sublattice long-range magnetic order. Beyond 4 GPa, it enters a non-magnetic state. Notably, Bi5FeTi3O15 displays pressure-tunable magnetism in contrast to pressure-induced giant magnetism observed in its three-layer counterpart Bi3Fe2Ti2O11.

Hybrid methods combining integer programming and continuous optimization are used extensively in the shortest path framework, particularly in flight planning. This approach first generates rough paths via the shortest path algorithm and then refines them to minimize a cost functional through continuous optimization. Although widely adopted, there are limitations to understanding the accuracy of this approach. A key issue lies in the absence of standards for assessing the reliability of costs obtained from the hybrid method. To address this, a novel framework is proposed to estimate the maximum potential error in the cost functional caused by restricting the search space to discrete paths. A specific application to free-flight trajectory optimization demonstrates the efficacy of this framework, offering insights into (i) the influence of grid resolution and cost function parameters on the estimated and actual discrepancies, as well as (ii) the potential for entirely skipping the continuous optimization stage.

Observations from nearby supernovias and the light curves of rare astrophysical sources, including the merger of neutron stars that produced both a short gamma-ray burst and a Type Ia-like supernova explosion, reveal the existence of intense shockwaves in the universe's early moments. By utilizing a simple one-dimensional hydrodynamic model of a spherical void in a flat, expanding universe, we found that a rapidly expanding surface wave is generated when a shockwave front moves through matter with varying densities. This model provides a straightforward mechanism for generating intense shockwaves and may offer insights into the origin of short gamma-ray bursts, although further research and high-cadence, multi-wavelength observations are necessary to fully understand this phenomenon.

Using 3.2 inverse femtobarns of $b$-hadron collision data collected by the LHCb collaboration at center-of-mass energies of 13 and 13.6 teraelectronvolts, the measurement of the differential decay rate for the process $B_s^0\rightarrow D_s^{*-}\mu^{+}\nu_{\mu}$ as a function of the squared mass of the $D_s^{-}\mu^{-}$ system has been thoroughly analyzed. By fully reconstructing the $D_s^{-}$ meson and accounting for the undetected neutrino, multiple measurements of the decay rate's slope parameters are updated, reducing the combined uncertainty to $10^{-4}$ or better. Additionally, after accounting for the polarization of the $D_s^{*-}$, the corresponding slope parameters for its decay are also updated.

A previous classification of polynomial solutions to the Schrödinger equation with regular potential was revisited, focusing on both bounded and unbounded domains. An effort was made to extend the theory to describe accurate approximations of unbounded domain solutions using linear combinations of states that are defined within bounded domains. Specifically, it was demonstrated that such combinations could effectively capture the characteristics of scattering states, including their energy and phase shifts. Furthermore, this study effort led to discovery of conditions, free from monodromy, that are essential for obtaining polynomial solutions. These conditions were also applied to investigate potential functions, such as P\"oschl-Teller, which support such solutions.

When an adhesive tape is peeled from a surface, its speed varies at different moments and speeds as it separates. To understand this behavior better, we investigated how sudden releases affect the time it takes for the tape to separate completely. Our study involved recording the durations between each micro-slips event and identifying patterns in the data through statistical analysis. Our results indicate that the distribution of these events follows a specific pattern and that sudden releases are strongly influenced by previous releases. This mutual predictability provides evidence for hidden variables in the system, in contrast to the idea of randomness. Our proposed model suggests that information about internal stresses is what drives this predictability.

Our theoretical analysis suggests that in two-dimensional superconductors, fluctuations can cause additional symmetry-breaking, resulting in the development of vortices at a specific transition temperature above the critical point, and a more complex behavior of the BCS state near this point, characterized by a disorder-driven unbinding of pairs. In a planar Josephson junction or a SQUIRD, the application of magnetic fields or voltage can induce the formation of vortices. To reflect this complex behavior theoretically, we created a generalized Ginzburg-Landau model that incorporates disordered terms and an explicit term representing vortex-antivortex interactions. From this model, we derived a vortex critical point that occurs at a specific temperature or field/voltage, and found it to be associated with a singular behavior of the superconducting order parameter and a divergence of the junction's resistance. Notably, this singular resistance behavior is distinct from the conventional linear relationship. Simulations of a 2D dirty niobium film, which we observed experimentally, revealed a specific temperature at which vortices start to appear, and the Generalized Ginzburg-Landau model, which incorporated vortex interactions, accurately predicted the observed behavior of the superconducting resistance, in contrast to the conventional model.

We modify the Einstein-Cartan theory by adding a term representing the cosmic ether, which is analogous to the $\theta_{\mu\nabla\rho}\epsilon^{\rho\sigma\alpha\beta}\nabla_\alpha R_\beta$ interaction in a non-abelian gauge theory. By utilizing a temperature-based method to examine various vacuums, we find that this ether term generates an effective potential with specific properties. These effective potentials can be used to investigate the phase transitions that occur in non-abelian thermodynamics, particularly in terms of their temperature and symmetry-breaking aspects. Our theoretical framework is then applied to examine the dynamics of neutron stars and the early universe's evolution, specifically focusing on its cooling processes.

We present a method for calculating the expected cost of delta-hedging a stock option by accounting for market impact, providing an efficient solution to the challenging problem of delta-hedging cost for options. Specifically, we are able to hedge the option using a pre-determined amount of money rather than continuously. We develop a formula that represents the hedging cost as a function of the underlying asset's price, enabling us to evaluate the hedging cost at any given price. This approach is applicable to various types of underlying assets. We validate our method through stock index option data, showing that our estimated hedging costs are closely aligned with actual market-hedged prices.

We investigate the effective properties of a composite material whose constituents have extremely varied contrast properties, arranged in a periodic pattern on separate, interlocking periodic grids that shift relative to one another with a small scale parameter, $\varepsilon$. The material is subject to a compatibility condition arising from a divergence constraint, which ensures the matrix and inclusion phases form closed curves within each unit cell. Due to the high contrast and increasing density of the material components as $\varepsilon approaches zero$, the effective properties are heavily dependent on the relative grid alignment parameter and can only be defined in specific ways allowed by the connectivity condition. The study derives formulas for two-dimensional cases with specific algebra equations, resolving issues with differential constraints through a dual-space approach Albrecht, Dumann, Kohn, Mandel (2019).

We utilized new measurements from the Subaru Prime Focus Camera Deep Survey to determine the flux fraction of tidal features surrounding early-type galaxies. By comparing this to the total halo of these galaxies, we established the extent of their influence. Utilating the HSCSS database, which comprises over 150,000 examples, we were able to make statistically significant observations, particularly for massive galaxies with masses greater than $10^{11} M_{\odot}$. In this range, we found that nearly 80% of galaxies displayed tidal features that accounted for less than 10% of the total light. By combining these data with existing surveys, which cover $z < 0.15$, we calculated the merger rate of massive galaxies to be at least 10-20% of galaxies with masses greater than $10^{11} M_{\odot} * h^{-3} M_{\odot}$ per billion years. This is a surprisingly elevated merger rate for galaxies of this mass. It implies that a substantial portion of galaxies, greater than 50%, greater than 75%, and potentially as much as 88% of galaxies with masses greater than $10^{11} M_{\odot} * h^{-3} M_{\odot} $ should exhibit tidal features and constitute an excessive amount of quiescent galaxies with stellar masses greater than $10^{11} M

Research on intergenerational mobility often reveals that children from disadvantaged backgrounds tend to stay in the same socioeconomic status as their parents, while those from affluent families are more likely to advance to a higher socioeconomic status. This suggests that individuals from middle-class backgrounds have fewer opportunities for social advancement or stagnation compared to their counterparts from wealthy families. To address this disparity, we develop a computer-based, intergenerational mobility model that accounts for various factors including initial resources available to individuals, opportunities for employment, and influences from family examples. The dynamic nature of this model is featured through a 10-year simulation, during which individuals from different socioeconomic backgrounds are categorized into three groups. It is shown that purely individual-centric approaches using threshold-based decision-making do not fully capture the observed mobility patterns, whereas wealth accumulation influenced by the actions of wealthy families and middle-class counterparts can effectively reproduce these patterns. Moreover, we explore potential policy options aimed at enhancing mobility among lower-middle-class families in our model.

The development of high-power lasers has made significant breakthroughs across various fields such as atomic and molecular research, precision processing, and advanced imaging. Consequently, reverse engineering laser systems with complex configurations and modified or damaged optical components has been made feasible and scientifically valuable. This paper outlines the principles of reverse engineering laser systems, emphasizing the use of advanced laser measurement techniques such as stochastic metrology, multi-wavelength, and polarization measurement techniques. A case study involving the analysis of a high-power laser measurement system is used to illustrate the development, measurement, and evaluation processes, demonstrating the applicability of this approach in understanding high-power laser systems.

We prove that for $1 < p < 2$, if a subset $K$ of $\ell_p$ has diameter $d$ and does not contain contractible paths, then there is a map from $K$ to a set that is $\varepsilon$-isometric and lies within a space with dimension less than that required to demonstrate $K$'s incompressibility, with $\varepsilon$ depending only on $p$.

In the "brightness scan" technique, a deliberate variation of beam brightness is conducted at a specific location to beam diagnostics instruments. These instruments could be beam current transformers, beam profile monitors, or other similar devices. The intended fluctuations of beam brightness are achieved by adjusting two independent parameters: beam phase-space area and angular divergence. Notably, changing the beam phase-space area has an equivalent effect on brightness, so it can be substituted for variations in divergence. A method is proposed to execute this beam brightness variation scheme using independent controls. Furthermore, through analytical calculations and numerical simulations, the effects of brightness scans on beam diagnostics devices are examined. It is discovered that certain beam monitoring devices, like beam profile monitors, are influenced by beam variance rather than divergence. As a result, specific techniques must be adopted to carry out brightness scans effectively. Alternatively, other beam monitoring devices remain largely unaffected by these changes in beam parameters. Brightness scans can provide valuable information about other beam properties, including central moments and other characteristics. Therefore, additional considerations must be taken into account when conducting these scans. A mathematical framework for modeling brightness scans incorporates nonstationary effects and enables the beam brightness to be determined from beam monitoring data. This approach uses a set of 2D beam propagation equations to capture nonstationary dynamics. Ultimately, brightness scans prove to be a useful tool in enhancing beam diagnostics.

This paper presents a distributed optimization algorithm that enables each participant in a network to efficiently update their local variables and contribute to an optimal solution, even when some participants have malicious intentions. A technical approach is outlined to identify and isolate these malicious participants by analyzing the frequency of their attacks and isolating the affected sub-networks to prevent further spread. Furthermore, the article combines this attack detection strategy with an existing method to achieve convergence to an optimal solution, despite the presence of attacked edges in the network. Finally, the proposed approach is validated through numerical experiments that demonstrate its effectiveness and efficiency.

We have developed a flexible framework that utilizes open-source libraries including s4, s4cutny, and astropy to cut and smooth the sky, emulating the cosmic microwave background observational processes. This framework allows for accurate prediction of the impact of various instrumental factors, such as beam, sensitivity, and sky coverage errors on the reconstruction of the reionization and primary component of the cosmic microwave background differential temperature power spectrum and the resulting parameter constraints.

In NLP, using pre-trained language models (PLMs) to enhance or substitute human knowledge is becoming a prevalent trend. To analyze how PLMs influence human word ordering tasks, we designed an experiment where participants sort scrambled words into meaningful sentences, some of which are seen after being processed by the BART PLM. We discovered that the word coloring by BART, where words are influenced by their context, does not significantly aid people in understanding the text. Furthermore, we found that people's word ordering abilities remain largely unaffected by the additional context provided by BART, with their performance consistently high regardless of whether words are sorted into meaningful sentences or random arrangements. Inspections of people's thinking processes revealed that they rely more on semantic coherence and syntactic structure, generated by BART, to arrive at their conclusions. These findings indicate that people utilize the semantic information and logical connections of sentences, which are identified and classified by BART, to achieve excellent word ordering results.

Deepfakes are indistinguishable fake videos that pose threats in areas such as personal security and content authenticity. As deepfake generation techniques become more sophisticated, our ability to detect them is being challenged. Recent frameworks centered on distribution matching have shown promise in identifying deepfakes, yet they struggle with inconsistencies due to uncertainties arising from variations in real source images and encoder outputs. In a bid to tackle these limitations, we introduce a novel framework called the MD-CSDNetwork, which incorporates cross-stitch networks to automatically learn and incorporate complementary information from real and forged data. This framework leverages the additional useful features in real and forged images to enrich the primary distribution to enhance detection performance. Moreover, it reduces inconsistencies stemming from real data differences and encoder-generated sources. Thorough experiments and comparative analyses on multiple datasets showcase that MD-CSDNetwork achieves superior accuracy and robustness when detecting deepfakes.

Current research into low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes is focused on codes that are independent of their channel, but there's a lack of studies on LDPC codes with correlated check nodes, especially in the context of memoryless deletion channels. In order to analyze the decoding performance of LDPC codes under binary deletion channels, a new method is required, as conventional approaches are rendered ineffective due to the check nodes' dependence. This paper introduces an extension to the message-passing decoding algorithm suitable for correlated LDPC codes and establishes a framework for assessing decoding success based on the correlation patterns within the parity-check matrix. In particular, we developed a correlation-aware min-sum decoding algorithm, modifying the decoding process to incorporate the patterns of check-node correlation. We then derived a decoding success criterion known as the generalized normal approximation, which predicts the code's behavior under binary deletion channels. Finally, the generalised normal approximation was validated through numerical experiments on several types of LDPC codes with varying check-node correlation patterns.

A novel, highly secure, and user-friendly decoy-state QKD algorithm was proposed by us, which incorporates partial phase randomization to counterattack methods. Analytical calculations demonstrated that the new scheme achieves the same security as the original BB84 protocol without needing to consider photon number separation attacks. Furthermore, the new scheme yields a higher key allocation rate than traditional multi-intensity vacuum-state decoy protocols. Moreover, it can accomplish this outcome with partial phase randomization, reducing the necessity for random phase modulation and thus lowering the attack risk of leakage Decoy-state QKD was then analyzed practically, but the new scheme retained its outstanding performance.

To effectively manage and maintain 5G core network performance, novel monitoring and corrective measures are necessary. This paper outlines recommended approaches for netflex traffic management, network configuration optimization, and fault rectification. Key topics discussed include graph algorithm modifications for improved netflex stability, self-adjusting routing protocols, and adaptive maximum flow netflex stability management. By leveraging machine learning for core network analysis and management, we can achieve optimal performance and minimize stability fluctuations in netflex systems.

In 1906, mathematician Menger initiated a rigorous mathematical examination of geometry by creating an abstract framework for geometry based on elements and distances. He later expanded this framework in 1928 to incorporate geometry based on elements and angles. Although Menger formulated several axioms for this new geometry, including the development of angle modules, he failed to provide their existence proof. Furthermore, he investigated specific geometric space types based on postulated angle properties but with undefined measures. Given that Menger's angle geometry concepts lack explicit definition in R^n, this research establishes foundational axioms for geometry within standard Euclidean space, including a specific subclass characterized by certain angle restrictions. The proof of geometry subspace existence is achieved through mathematical induction and transformation techniques, ultimately enabling the size classification of geometry classes and offering insights into their intrinsic dimensions through density measurement.

We investigate the relationship between successive minima and lattice theory in number fields, and our research may contribute to proving the finiteness of curves with bounded successive minima ratios. This connection led us to derive improved bounds on the successive minima of order rings, particularly for Gaussian integers and some quadratic fields. Additionally, we obtained new bounds on the quadratic field ring R = Z[√-3]. These findings were accompanied by derivation of relevant inequalities and relations.

We utilize 1-d fs/ps hybrid rotational coherent anti-Stokes Raman spectroscopy with dual probes to analyze gas properties. This technique enables the measurement of temperature, pressure, and non-invasive identification of oxygen and nitrogen in a single experiment. By leveraging one-dimensional spectra, it is possible to distinguish between similar molecules and improve the precision of gas property measurements. The proposed method involves using sum-frequency generation to create distinct spectral ranges that resolve the O2/nitrogen spectra in the 1550 nm range. A crucial aspect of this approach is ensuring phase stability between the femtosecond and picosecond probes to maintain a strong and reliable signal. The experiment demonstrates simultaneous detection of multiple gases in a single shot, as well as precise measurements of gas pressure. Additionally, various strategies to minimize errors and improve the accuracy of these measurements are explored. Ultimately, this research paves the way for real-time, highly-resolved imaging of gas properties using high-speed cameras or spatial light modulators.

Scientists believe that in young solar disks, vertical vortex structures called "ripple-rolls" can create calm zones that trap dust and create dust piles, potentially starting the formation of planets. A specific ripple-rolls formation can lead to a tube-like structure that grows larger due to material flowing into it from the surrounding disk. These formations can also produce high levels of heat through friction, which could influence how dust clumps together to form planets. Using computer simulations, researchers are studying how these vortex structures affect the flow of gas and the movement of dust in the outskirts of young solar disks. They found that certain conditions within these formations can cause dust to settle into layers, creating a more planar environment, while forming strong winds within the vortex itself could result in the accumulation of dust into pronounced structures, potentially shaping the future of planet formation.

A new phenomenon, known as upstream neutral modes (UNMs), has been identified in the context of long non-equilibrium transport and observed experimentally in a hybrid superconductor-semiconductor two-dimensional system. These modes, which are equivalent to upstream neutral modes, have a unique stability that allows them to persist even in the presence of weak backscattering. It has been demonstrated numerically and verified through a lattice model that these neutral modes generate an excess voltage at the sample edges due to a non-reciprocal drift of electrons in response to an applied bias. Notably, this effect is not influenced by the chemical potential of the upstream filled edge channels and enables precise detection of the neutral modes' charge carrier densities. As such, UNMs have the potential to contribute to non-equilibrium transport and may contribute to achieving quantum coherence necessary for non-dissipative transport of neutral modes in the form of the upstream neutral currents.

We introduce novel formulas for the cluster monomial correspondence in quantum clusters that apply to arbitrary coefficients, quantization parameters, and deformations. For type A cases, we derive expressions for initial cluster $R$-matrices which are unitary, rational matrices with integer entries when quantized. These formulas can be used to prove the correspondence for type A cases and provide concrete computations for difficult algebraic elements such as primitive parts of quantum cluster algebras and quantum Fock-Goncharov parity checks.

In our research paper, we tackle the distributionally robust decentralized learning problem. This problem is characterized by multiple trainers who use the same model but have data that follows different statistical distributions, resulting in a non-i.i.d. setting. Each trainer is also connected to a network that changes over time. To address this challenge, we introduce a new algorithm called DR-SGD, which allows for decentralized and distributed training without a central coordinator. This algorithm is named after the robust nature of it, enabling trainers to reach a consensus on a single model through communication with their neighboring nodes. We further develop a communication-efficient variation of the algorithm, allowing trainers to reach near-optimal performance on their loss functions. Our experiments show that DR-SGD outperforms other decentralized learning approaches in terms of accuracy. This new method achieves a communication complexity better than previous ones in the change-over-time graph setting, and in fact, it surpasses the theoretical optimum in some cases.

We have conducted an extensive review of research and review articles on mathematical models that model the behavior of magnetic elements in computer storage devices. Models are used to model hard-drives, tape drives, and disk drives. We also discuss a new type of modeling approach used for solid-state drives.

This paper examines the initial state evolution of high-energy proton-proton collisions, leading to the formation of quark-gluon plasma and the impact on forward jet production, considering various theoretical uncertainties including scale variations, nuclear PDF sets, and medium temperature fluctuations. Our analysis indicates that the observed jet data can be explained by varying the initial state within reasonable limits, and the impact of temperature fluctuations on jet energy loss can be effectively managed within the Karmakar-McLerran framework by accounting for the natural variations in the initial state.

This paper delves into the intricate workings of Forsage, a fraudulent investment platform that generated over $360 million in revenue between 2019 and 2021, primarily based in Spain. Forsage operated through the use of up to 120 deceptive smart contracts on the Ethereum blockchain. By analyzing Forsage's code, we uncovered its pyramidal structure and created a mathematical model to represent its workings. Furthermore, we examined the potential impacts of regulatory measures on such schemes.

We have conducted an in-depth examination of 19 previously identified and newly discovered globular clusters within the Milky Way's bulge region. These were located using data from the VISTA Variable Objects in the Southern Sky and VISTA Infrared Variable Survey, which utilized infrared imagery. Specifically, we found that the 19 clusters were between 2.4 and 8.4 kiloparsecs from the galactic center, with ages ranging from 8.6 billion to 12.8 billion years old and metal content varying from -1.39 to -0.55. Notably, the clusters with the highest metal content were found in close proximity to the galactic center. We also found that 14 clusters with sufficient data for analysis followed the trend of showing higher densities near the center. We believe that a significant number of clusters will be discovered as we continue to analyze more regions of the Southern Sky using these same survey techniques.

We examine the dynamics of high-transverse-momentum hadrons inside a proton, which occurs when a heavy, off-shell quark in the proton collides with another proton, a process known as the色-charge-diffusion process. This phenomenon is beyond the scope of traditional parton distribution theory and necessitates an extension of Quantum Chromodynamics to incorporate color-diffusion theory. By constructing a coherent framework for color-diffusion theory in the quark-boson-scattering process, we investigate its impact on exclusive reactions, such as lepton production, in hadron-hadron collisions. We derive the factorization and rapidity-evolution equations for this process in a perturbative format and perform numerical calculations using the NNPDF and GRV parton distribution functions, as well as the Hessian and GRV fragmentation functions. Our results indicate that this process could be experimentally observable in certain regions of phase space, such as those accessible in Drell-Yan reactions at the LHC and the Large Hadron Electron Collider at low invariant masses.

The accuracy of density functional theory is compromised by approximations used for electron-hole interactions and the electron-electron ground state model. Despite these limitations, such approximations are standard in DF-TB calculations. To investigate the effect of these approximations on conductivity, researchers have developed two models: one that replicates the DF-SOKSDA equation and another that uses a stochastic approach. These synthetic models were applied to benzene and graphite, resulting in conductivity spectra that differed when using the DF model and stochastic model, with the DF model producing conductive outcomes that were also non-Kramers-Crystal, while the stochastic model produced conductive results that were non-integer.

Tensor network states are widely used in representing many-body systems because they can efficiently capture some of the key correlations that occur between particles. Within this category, the holographic multiscale entangle renormalization ansatz (MEMA) state stands out due to its connection to gravity through the AdS/CFT correspondence, which allows it to provide an accurate description of critical systems. Nevertheless, while the standard MERA design does incorporate an entanglement correction correction code (ECC) capability within specific ranges, it falls short of exhibiting complete double symmetry. In contrast, a newly developed highly symmetric hyper-invariant MERA (hi-MERA) structure, while maintaining its intricate double network architecture, lacks the necessary simplicity to serve as a fully capable holographic ECC.

A computational study was conducted on retinal's photoisomerization using a quantum mechanical/molecular mechanical (QM/MM) approach, specifically examining how the surrounding environment of opsin affects the photoisomerization process. Retinal is composed of a chromophore surrounded by a protein matrix, and its photoisomerization is critical to vision as it underpins the process in proteins like opsin and rhodopsin. By creating a series of models with gradually increasing distortion of the chromophore by the protein, researchers found that the surrounding environment has a profound impact on the efficiency of retinal's photoisomerization. In isolated gas-phase retinal, multiple conversion pathways are accessible, but as the protein tightens its grip on the chromophore, it restricts motion and forces retinal into an excited-state conical intersection, which is the most efficient route for converting energy into heat. This mechanism aligns with the photoisomerization processes observed in rhodopsin and 5-hydroxytryptophan-opsin. A novel and previously unreported phenomenon was also discovered - extreme parametric reactivity - where subtle shifts in the protein's interaction with the chromophore can induce abrupt changes in the photoisomerization pathway and retinal's ability to initiate the process.

Deep-learning methods such as Convolutional Neural Networks and Recurrent Neural Networks have seen significant success in process mining. To explore the potential of a novel approach, this study examines a different type of deep learning architecture called a Self-Attention-based Deep Learning model. Comparing the traditional and innovative models, researchers concluded that the attention-based method yields more accurate results than its traditional counterpart.

Earthquakes cause significant damage and many casualties, necessitating an examination of their repercussions on both humans and societies. Social media platforms play a crucial role in reflecting public opinions and can be utilized for tracking these effects. We utilize Twitter data to analyze public sentiment surrounding the impact of earthquakes, specifically exploring how they affect individuals and drive their behavior both before and after an event. We gather Twitter messages from worldwide, Turkish, and Izmir regions and examine how different populations are affected by earthquakes in 2012 and 2020. Our findings reveal that while the event in Izmir altered pre-event patterns, post-event data showed nearly identical outcomes to previous events.

A comprehensive analysis of a historically significant solar flare, a 2.6 GBa cosmic ray event on AD Leo, has been performed on the impact of particle radiation on the host star, which occurred on April 12, 1985. Due to the scarcity of observational data from active M-dwarf stars in the near-ultraviolet (UV) spectrum during this period, we utilized a near-UV continuum simulation based on the updated version of the SPoTS code. By comparing the simulated results with available archival data from the Kepler and TESS space telescopes, we found that this flare was responsible for increasing the near-UV flux by a factor of 1000000, which in turn led to a 1000-fold increase in host star heating and a corresponding 100-fold increase in near-UV photon flux. We also estimated that this significant increase in particle radiation may have had a 100-fold increase in host star photoevaporation rate. However, due to a 1000000-fold decrease in photoionization heating efficiency, the net effect on photoevaporation rate was found to be 100 times, which would lead to a 10 seconds increase in system lifetime. Additionally, we also discuss the implications of this event on habitable exoplanets and found that Earth-like conditions on any such planet would have been significantly altered by this significant increase in particle heating and photo

This analysis focuses on the effects of PT-symmetry in periodic structures comprising PT-symmetric and symmetric units, with applications to photonic crystals and waveguide arrays.
